DETAILED ACTION
This communication is a first office action on the merits. All currently pending claims have been considered below. The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Drawings
Figure 2 should be designated by a legend such as --Prior Art-- because only that which is old is illustrated. See MPEP § 608.02(g). The specification describes figure 2 as a conventional geothermal power generation system (¶ 19).
Corrected drawings in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. The replacement sheet(s) should be labeled “Replacement Sheet” in the page header (as per 37 CFR 1.84(c)) so as not to obstruct any portion of the drawing figures. If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
Claims 1-12 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, regards as the invention.
Claim 1 recites inter alia providing a flow of a first fluid into the borehole [thereby causing] a rock layer to be maintained around a portion of the borehole located within the magma reservoir.
The examiner holds this to be indefinite because the use of maintained implies, but does not clearly recite, that the rock layer… within the magma reservoir is previously created and already exists. However, in light of the specification, it appears that the first fluid creates this rock layer. This interpretation is further supported by dependent claim 11 which recites stopping the flow of the first fluid… causes the rock layer formed by the first fluid to melt… However parent claim 1 does not recite the first fluid forming the rock layer.
The examiner respectfully suggests the phrase be changed to … causes a rock layer to be formed and maintained from the magma around a portion of the borehole… or some grammatic variation thereof. Claims 2-12 depend from claim 1.
Claim 8 recites the first fluid is a drilling or cooling fluid. First, this is simply a change in nomenclature only. Neither drilling or cooling fluid convey any kind of new limitation per se from the generic recitation of first fluid. No drilling is recited in any of the claims, and claim 1 is conspicuously worded so as to not recite cooling the magma, for example.
Second, a primary purpose of drilling fluid is to cool the drilling structure, as is exceedingly well understood.
Finally, any fluid can be drilling or cooling fluid as currently recited. In other words, what is encompassed / allowed by a first fluid that is excluded by changing first fluid to a drilling or cooling fluid.
Claim 11 is held as indefinite for the phrase the rock layer formed by the first fluid. This does not have basis in parent claim 1, as similarly discussed in the 112(b) rejection of claim 1 above. Correction of claim 1 as discussed above would obviate this rejection of claim 11. Claim 12 depends from claim 11.
Claim 20 recites the first fluid is a drilling or cooling fluid which is held as indefinite as similarly described for claim 8 above.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 102
The following is a quotation of the appropriate paragraphs of 35 U.S.C. 102 that form the basis for the rejections under this section made in this Office action:
A person shall be entitled to a patent unless –
(a)(1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
Claims 13, 14, 16-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by US 3,398,794 (Fox).
Independent claim 13. Fox discloses a process (running large diameter casing - title), comprising:
preparing a borehole extending downward from a surface (10, fig 1; also clearly shown in fig 2);
providing a flow of a first fluid into the borehole (water 32 is added to the desired level - col 4:71-72);
lowering a casing into the borehole (When it is desired to run casing 12… - col 3:25); and
providing a second fluid into the casing (if the buoyancy should be reduced to permit the casing to sink, water is injected through the same, or a second conduit, into the compartment to effect such change in buoyancy - col 2:35-38), thereby causing the casing to sink into a volume of the first fluid within the borehole (ibid; figs 1 & 2).
Claim 14. The process of Claim 13, wherein the casing comprises a cylindrical body with an open end and a closed end (Figs 1 & 2 both show a cylindrical casing with a closed lower end. Relief valve 44 in fig 1 is not excluded by this as the valve closes the lower end. Fig 2 shows a fully closed lower end).
Claim 16. The process of Claim 13, further comprising, prior to providing the second fluid into the casing, determining that the casing is moving in a downward direction at less than a threshold speed (The supported weight determines the downward movement, and [t]he proper amount of water injected into the compartments can be determined by merely observing the weight of the casing on the supporting derrick and adding or removing water from such compartments to maintain the desired weight - col 4:11-15. In other words, less than the desired weight directly correlates to too little downward movement, and water is added directly responsive to this to permit the casing to sink - col 2:35-36).
Claim 17. The process of Claim 16, further comprising, prior to providing the second fluid into the casing, determining that a target depth of the casing has not been reached (The second fluid is added [w]hen it is desired to run casing 12 - col 3:25-52 - which is clearly and inherently before the casing a reached a target depth. The second fluid is stopped [w]hen the casing has been run to its total depth - col 2:41-42).
Claim 18. The process of Claim 13, further comprising providing the second fluid into the casing at a predetermined flow rate (predetermined to maintain the desired weight - col 4:8-15 - which is pre-calculated: col 4:1-7. In other words, the desired buoyancy and desired weight, which are predetermined as cited above, determine the rate the fluid is added as the casing is lowered to maintain fluid pressure: claim 1. In other words predetermined flow rate does not require steady / static / constant rate. The second fluid is not added haphazardly or randomly, but rather specifically based of predetermined criteria).
Claim 19. The process of Claim 13, further comprising providing a predetermined volume of the second fluid into the casing (injecting the proper amount of water into compartments 18 and 26, the desired buoyant effect is readily obtained from the casing 12 so that it can be lowered to the bottom of the well bore. The proper amount of water injected into the compartments can be determined by merely observing the weight of the casing on the supporting derrick and adding or removing water from such compartments to maintain the desired weight - col 4:8-14), the predetermined volume sufficient to cause lowering of the casing to a target depth within the borehole (ibid).
Claim 20. The process of Claim 13, wherein the first fluid is a drilling or cooling fluid (water 32 may be both a drilling fluid and/or a cooling fluid).
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claim 1-12 & 15 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over US 3,398,794 (Fox) in view of the NPL Magma Energy Research Project, 1982 (henceforth Magma NPL). Applicant provided a copy of the Magma NPL in the IDS filed 7/31/2023. The examiner cites the page numbers as-written in the document.
Claim 15. Fox discloses all the limitations of the parent claim but does not disclose continuously providing the flow of the first fluid into the borehole at least until the casing is lowered to a target depth.
However, the Magma NPL teaches the continuous circulation of cooling drilling fluid to form a wellbore in a magma formation by using high-velocity and high-volume jets of cooling water from the face of the bit to cool the molten rock ahead of the bit sufficiently so that it may be drilled (page 16, left column, first full ¶). Without a continuous supply, the cooled area will melt and must be re-cooled (page 16, right column, second to last ¶). However, continuously providing the flow of the first fluid into the borehole will be kept open and stable as long as desired by cooling with a stream of water from the surface (ibid).
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to sink the casing taught by Fox into magma by continuously circulating the first fluid as taught by the Magma NPL. First, Fox is clear that the casing may be used in a wide variety of applications, including deep drilling (col 4:57-60). Second, the Magma NPL is clear that damage the equipment was minimal… if a continuous flow of coolant was maintained (page 16, right column, third to last ¶). Finally, the use in a magma formation allows for substantial geothermal energy to be tapped (Magma NPL, ¶ bridging pages 7 & 8).
Independent claim 1. Fox discloses a process (running large diameter casing - title), comprising:
preparing a borehole extending downward from a surface (10, fig 1; also clearly shown in fig 2);
providing a flow of a first fluid into the borehole (water 32 is added to the desired level - col 4:71-72);
lowering a casing into the borehole (When it is desired to run casing 12… - col 3:25); and
providing a second fluid into the casing (if the buoyancy should be reduced to permit the casing to sink, water is injected through the same, or a second conduit, into the compartment to effect such change in buoyancy - col 2:35-38), thereby causing the casing to sink into a volume of the first fluid within the borehole (ibid; figs 1 & 2).
Fox is silent as to providing the first fluid into the borehole to cause a rock layer to be [formed] around a portion of the borehole located within a magma reservoir.
However, the Magma NPL teaches the continuous circulation of cooling drilling fluid to form a wellbore in a magma formation by using high-velocity and high-volume jets of cooling water from the face of the bit to cool the molten rock ahead of the bit sufficiently so that it may be drilled (page 16, left column, first full ¶). Without a continuous supply, the cooled area will melt and must be re-cooled (page 16, right column, second to last ¶). However, continuously providing the flow of the first fluid into the borehole will be kept open and stable as long as desired by cooling with a stream of water from the surface (ibid).
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time of filing to sink the casing taught by Fox into magma by continuously circulating the first fluid as taught by the Magma NPL. First, Fox is clear that the casing may be used in a wide variety of applications, including deep drilling (col 4:57-60). Second, the Magma NPL is clear that damage the equipment was minimal… if a continuous flow of coolant was maintained (page 16, right column, third to last ¶). Finally, the use in a magma formation allows for substantial geothermal energy to be tapped (Magma NPL, ¶ bridging pages 7 & 8).
Dependent claims 2-8 are the same as dependent claims 14-20, respectively, and are similarly rejected as described for those claims above, respectfully not repeated again here.
Claim 9. The process of Claim 1, further comprising providing the flow of that first fluid into the borehole at a flow rate sufficient to maintain a volume of the first fluid at or above a ceiling of the magma reservoir (Magma NPL: page 16, right column. If the first fluid does not extend to or above a ceiling of the magma reservoir, it will melt and collapse onto the string. Further, it is conventional & well understood drilling practice to fill the borehole will the drilling fluid to prevent the borehole from collapsing).
Claim 10. The process of Claim 9, further comprising, after determining that the casing reaches a target depth, stopping the flow of the first fluid into the borehole (logically follows from the Magma NPL that, when the casing is placed, the circulation of cooling fluid is stopped: page 16, right column).
Claim 11. The process of Claim 10, wherein stopping the flow of the first fluid into the borehole causes the rock layer formed by the first fluid to melt and magma within the magma reservoir (Magma NPL, page 16, right column, last ¶) to contact at least a portion of an outer surface of the casing within the borehole (naturally follows that if the magma will contact the bit and string as taught by the Magma NPL, it will likewise contact the casing of Fox once in the hole).
Claim 12. The process of Claim 11, further comprising providing a flow of the second fluid or another fluid through the casing, thereby causing a new rock layer to form proximate the outer surface of the casing within the magma reservoir (the reopened hole could be kept open and stable by reintroducing the coolant flow from above - Magma NPL, page 16, right column, second to last ¶).
Conclusion
